quiz.q: Δv depends on the mass ratio through…
quiz.why: ln(m₀/m_f).

quiz.q: Staging helps because…
quiz.why: Empty tanks no longer need accelerating.

quiz.q: To lift off, thrust-to-weight must be…
quiz.why: Thrust must exceed weight.

quiz.q: The effective exhaust speed for I_sp = 300 s is about…
quiz.why: I_sp × g₀.

quiz.q: Rockets push against the air.
quiz.why: They work best in vacuum; they push on their own exhaust.

quiz.q: Double the propellant, double the Δv.
quiz.why: Δv grows with the logarithm of the mass ratio.

quiz.q: Orbit needs only 7.7 km/s of Δv.
quiz.why: Gravity and drag losses push the total to roughly 9.4 km/s.

quiz.q: An engine with I_sp = 450 s fires until m₀/m_f = 5. Find Δv. Give your answer in m/s.
A two-stage rocket: each stage has I_sp = 300 s and mass ratio 4. Find the total Δv. Give your answer in m/s.
quiz.why: ≈ 8,157 m/s, twice what one stage with mass ratio 4 gives.

quiz.q: Find Δv for I_sp = 311 s and m₀/m_f = 3. Give your answer in m/s.
A 500,000 kg rocket has 7.5 MN of thrust. Find T/W at liftoff.
What I_sp gives Δv = 3,000 m/s with mass ratio 2?
≈ 24.4 versus ≈ 8.4: about 96% versus 88% of the rocket must be propellant.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit. What mass ratio does a single stage need for 9.4 km/s with I_sp = 300 s? With 450 s?

quiz.q: Every Earth-observing satellite, from Landsat to the missions that track sea level and greenhouse gases, rides a rocket sized with this equation. It is why each kilogram of instrument is precious and why satellites are built to be light.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Our Delta-v calculator lets you run the same numbers for real missions.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: A rocket carries all its propellant, fuel and oxidizer. Its thrust is F = ṁv_e + (p_e − p_a)A_e.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: The ideal rocket equation: Δv = v_e ln(m₀/m_f), with v_e = I_sp g₀. Speed grows only with the logarithm of the mass ratio.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Reaching low Earth orbit takes roughly 9.4 km/s of Δv once gravity and drag losses are included, so most of a launch vehicle’s mass is propellant.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Staging drops empty tanks and engines so later stages do not carry dead weight.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.

quiz.q: Thrust-to-weight ratio must exceed 1 to lift off.
quiz.why: This is stated in the unit.
